accepted.name: ci_excludes_zero
accepted.description: Whether the reported confidence interval lies entirely on one side of zero, i.e. the analysis is significant by the interval for a difference-type estimate (mean difference, change from baseline, risk difference).
accepted.units: indicator (0/1; 2 only if the limits are stored out of order)
accepted.why_it_matters: Covers the ~18% of analyses with no p_value at all, where the interval is the only evidence recorded. Knowing that zero -- not any other number -- is the null value for a difference is exactly the domain fact a pairwise-difference generator cannot have. Rows with a null CI evaluate to 0, which is a genuine limitation: absent is not the same as covering zero.

accepted.name: ci_excludes_unity
accepted.description: The ratio-scale twin of the previous column: whether the interval excludes 1, the null value for an odds ratio, risk ratio, hazard ratio or rate ratio.
accepted.units: indicator (0/1; 2 only if the limits are stored out of order)
accepted.why_it_matters: param_type is free text with 5,251 variants, so a model cannot reliably tell a difference from a ratio; supplying both null-value tests lets it learn which one is informative per context. Testing an interval against 1 is nonsense for a difference and decisive for a ratio -- the whole point is that the constant encodes what the column IS.

accepted.name: ci_contains_estimate
accepted.description: Whether the reported point estimate actually falls inside its own reported confidence interval. A well-formed analysis always satisfies this; a 0 means the row was mis-entered, mis-parsed, or the three numbers refer to different quantities.
accepted.why_it_matters: A validity check, not an effect measure. Registries are self-reported and this table has ci_upper_limit values of 999999999 and ci_lower_limit of -1395694, so some fraction of rows are junk. Sites whose submissions are internally inconsistent are sites with weak data management, which predicts failure to hit endpoints. Everything the brute-force generator computes from those rows is noise; this column says which rows they are.

accepted.name: ae_incidence_smoothed
accepted.description: Jeffreys-smoothed incidence of the reported adverse event: the fraction of at-risk participants who experienced it, with the 0.5/1 prior that keeps the quantity finite and stable when the arm is small or empty. Capped at 2, a value reached only by impossible rows where affected exceeds at-risk.
accepted.units: fraction of participants (0-1 for well-formed rows)
accepted.why_it_matters: The raw ratio is undefined for the rows with subjects_at_risk = 0 and wildly unstable for the quartile of rows with fewer than 10 at risk -- a single event in a 2-person arm reads as a 50% incidence. The smoothed form is what an epidemiologist would actually compute, and adverse-event burden is the mechanism by which trials at a site stop early without a result.

accepted.name: ae_log_odds
accepted.description: Haldane-Anscombe corrected log-odds of the reported adverse event: log(affected / unaffected) with the standard 0.5 continuity correction applied to both cells, so zero-event and all-event arms remain finite.
accepted.why_it_matters: Log-odds is the scale on which event rates from arms of very different sizes are comparable and on which safety signals are conventionally pooled; a rate of 0.001 vs 0.01 is a full unit apart here but nearly indistinguishable as a raw fraction. The 0.5 correction is the standard fix for the median row, where subjects_affected is 1.

accepted.name: ae_report_precision
accepted.description: Binomial standard error of the smoothed incidence above: sqrt(p(1-p)/n). How much the reported safety rate could move if the same arm were run again.
accepted.why_it_matters: Turns a rate into a rate-plus-its-uncertainty. It is largest exactly where the reported incidence is least trustworthy -- mid-range rates in small arms -- and near zero for the large well-powered arms, letting a model discount a scary-looking 50% incidence that came from four people.

accepted.name: mdes_per_arm
accepted.description: Minimum detectable effect size: the smallest standardised effect (Cohen's d) this trial could detect at 80% power and a two-sided 0.05 test, given its enrollment split evenly across arms. Formula d = (z_0.975 + z_0.80) * sqrt(2/n_per_arm) = 3.96/sqrt(n_per_arm).
accepted.why_it_matters: This is the quantity a statistician computes before agreeing to run a trial, and it says what the trial is capable of finding rather than how big it is. The median study (60 participants, 2 arms) gets d = 0.72 -- it can only detect a large effect -- while a 1,000-person trial gets 0.18. A site whose portfolio is structurally unable to detect realistic effects will have a low success rate regardless of the science. Null wherever number_of_arms is null (24% of studies, mostly observational).

accepted.name: is_underpowered_comparative
accepted.description: Flags a study that has a comparison group yet enrolls fewer than 30 participants per arm -- below the conventional rule-of-thumb floor at which normal-approximation inference on a between-arm comparison is taken seriously.
accepted.why_it_matters: Being small is only a defect if you are trying to compare something: a 12-person single-arm pharmacokinetics study is fine, a 12-person two-arm efficacy trial is not. The flag depends on both columns jointly with a domain constant, which is precisely the distinction any pairwise ratio of enrollment and number_of_arms throws away. Given a median enrollment of 60, this fires on a large and genuinely distinguishable minority.

rejected.name: analysis_is_significant
rejected.description: Whether this reported statistical analysis cleared the conventional two-sided 0.05 significance threshold. A p-value is a measurement whose meaning is entirely defined by its comparison to a convention; the number itself is not the quantity anyone uses.
rejected.why_it_matters: This is the atom of trial success. A site's success rate is essentially the fraction of its past analyses that landed on the right side of 0.05, so a per-analysis significance flag on rows the site has already accumulated is the single most direct predictor available. Nulls (18% of rows) and the 19 negative p-values both evaluate to 0.
problems: |corr| 1.0000 with existing column `method_description` -- a rescaling of something the model already has

rejected.name: evidence_strength
rejected.description: Negative log p-value in nats: the strength of evidence against the null, on the scale where evidence adds up. Floored at p=1e-10 so exact zeros and the 19 negative values do not produce infinities.
rejected.why_it_matters: p=0.049 and p=0.0001 are the same success under a threshold but very different science. The log scale is the one on which p-values from independent analyses are comparable and combinable, so it separates a site that scrapes past 0.05 from one that produces decisive results. Values below 0 come from the dirty rows where p_value exceeds 1.
problems: |corr| 1.0000 with existing column `method` -- a rescaling of something the model already has

rejected.name: estimate_imprecision
rejected.description: Confidence-interval width expressed as a multiple of the effect size it brackets, log-compressed. A dimensionless coefficient-of-variation for the reported estimate: 0 means the interval is a point, ~0.7 means the interval is about as wide as the effect, large values mean the study measured essentially nothing.
rejected.why_it_matters: The raw CI width is meaningless without knowing the scale of the effect -- a width of 5 is tight for a blood-pressure change in mmHg and hopeless for an odds ratio. Dividing by the estimate is what makes width comparable across the 5,251 distinct param_types in this table, and imprecise sites are sites that will miss their endpoints next year.

rejected.name: z_from_ci
rejected.description: The z-statistic reconstructed from a reported confidence interval: 2 x midpoint divided by the implied standard error (width/3.92). Winsorised at +/-50 because some rows report a zero-width interval.
rejected.why_it_matters: It recovers the test statistic on the 63% of rows that carry an interval, including many where p_value is missing, and it is signed -- so it distinguishes an effect that favours the treatment from one that favours the control, which a p-value cannot. It is a ratio of a sum to a difference of two columns, which no pairwise generator produces.
